meta.title: How Spain Ruled the World, Then Lost Everything
meta.working_title: The Empire Built on a Mistake: Spain, 1492 to 1898
meta.device: A painted silver coin, the Spanish dollar (piece of eight), spins in the corner of every act. It shines brighter as the empire grows, is chipped by each bankruptcy, and at the end of 1898 falls flat and stops spinning. The parchment map from part 1 returns, now spreading Spanish gold across the Americas and the Pacific.
meta.style: 2D dynamic, locked Village Painterly look: 6-head characters from the village-cast rig (smooth tapered limbs, detailed 4-finger hands, nose below the eye line), in period costume (Castilian doublets and morions, Aztec and Inca dress, sailors, miners, 1890s uniforms). Highly detailed painted backgrounds with warm light and dynamic cast shadows: Seville's harbour, Tenochtitlan on its lake, the Andes, the red mountain of Potosi, galleons in storms, El Escorial, Havana harbour at night. Moving cameras, 3 to 5 parallax layers, characters acting in every shot, match-cut transitions. SFX under the VO; no music until combine.
meta.source: 'The Entire History of the Spanish Empire' plus the second half of 'The Entire History of Spain', fact-checked.

shots.vo: In the mountains of Bolivia there is a red mountain that, for about two centuries, produced a huge share of all the silver in the world.
shots.visual: The cone of Cerro Rico above Potosi, red and scarred, at sunrise; tiny mine entrances all over it.
shots.anim: Slow push toward the mountain; smoke from smelters; dust in the light.

shots.vo: That silver paid for armies, palaces and wars across three continents. It made Spain the first empire on which, people said, the sun never set.
shots.visual: Silver bars stacked on a ship's deck; the spinning silver coin flips into the corner.
shots.anim: Bars thud down; the coin spins up and settles in the corner.

shots.vo: And yet the king who owned all that silver went bankrupt four times.
shots.visual: Philip II at a desk piled with unpaid bills; a banker waits at the door.
shots.anim: Bills slide off the desk; the coin in the corner cracks.

shots.vo: It all began with a sailor who got lost. He was trying to reach India.
shots.visual: A small ship on an empty ocean; Columbus at the rail looking at a map of the wrong world.
shots.anim: Waves; the map in his hand shows Asia where America should be.

shots.visual: Title over a galleon sailing into a gold sunset.
shots.anim: Galleon crosses the frame; title fades up.

shots.vo: In 1492 Spain had just conquered Granada. Next door, Portugal was getting rich by sailing around Africa to reach the spices of Asia.
shots.visual: Map: a Portuguese route curls around Africa toward India; Spain sits idle.
shots.anim: Dotted line crawls around Africa; small spice sacks appear in India.

shots.vo: Christopher Columbus, a sailor from Genoa, had a different idea. Sail west, straight across the Atlantic, and you reach Asia faster.
shots.visual: Columbus in a court hall pointing at a globe; advisers shake their heads.
shots.anim: He spins the globe; advisers frown and mutter.

shots.vo: The experts said he was wrong, and they were right. He thought the world was much smaller than it is. Portugal said no. But Ferdinand and Isabella, flush from victory, said yes.
shots.visual: Close on the globe: Columbus's finger covers a short gap; a scholar's hand shows a much longer one.
shots.anim: Two hands measure the globe; the gap grows.

shots.vo: On the third of August 1492 he left Spain with three small ships, the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria, and about ninety men.
shots.visual: Three ships leave Palos harbour at dawn; families wave on the shore.
shots.anim: Sails fill; boats slide out past the camera.

shots.vo: After more than two months at sea, with the crew close to mutiny, a lookout saw land on the twelfth of October.
shots.visual: Night on deck: sailors argue with Columbus; then dawn, a lookout in the crow's nest points and shouts.
shots.anim: Tense lantern-lit argument; hard cut to the lookout's shout and a sunrise reveal of land.

shots.vo: It was an island in the Bahamas. Columbus believed he was near India, so he called the people he met Indians. The name stuck for five hundred years.
shots.visual: Columbus wading ashore with a flag; Taino people watching from the treeline.
shots.anim: He plants the flag; the Taino step forward cautiously.

shots.vo: To stop a war with Portugal, the two kingdoms signed the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 and split the world along a line in the Atlantic. Everything west for Spain, east for Portugal.
shots.visual: A ruler draws a vertical line down the Atlantic; colours split the world.
shots.anim: A quill draws the line; Spain's colour floods west. Brazil bulges east of the line for Portugal.

shots.vo: Columbus made four voyages and died in 1506, still insisting he had reached Asia.
shots.visual: An old Columbus in bed, papers and maps around him.
shots.anim: Candle burns low; a map slips from the bed.

shots.vo: The real riches were on the mainland. In central Mexico the Aztec Empire ruled from Tenochtitlan, a city of perhaps two hundred thousand people built on a lake.
shots.visual: Tenochtitlan: white temples, canals full of canoes, causeways across a blue lake, volcanoes behind.
shots.anim: Long glide across the lake; canoes move; temple smoke rises.

shots.vo: In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed on the coast with about five hundred men. He sank most of his own ships so nobody could go back.
shots.visual: Cortes on a beach, ships tilting into the water behind him; soldiers stare.
shots.anim: Masts lean and go under; soldiers' faces turn from sea to Cortes.

shots.vo: He had a secret weapon: a young Indigenous woman named Malintzin, who spoke Nahuatl and Maya and soon learned Spanish. She became his interpreter and adviser.
shots.visual: Malintzin standing between Cortes and a local chief, speaking to both.
shots.anim: She turns from one to the other; speech lines connect them.

shots.vo: His bigger weapon was the Aztecs' enemies. Peoples like the Tlaxcalans hated Aztec rule, and tens of thousands of them joined the Spanish.
shots.visual: Tlaxcalan warriors with feathered shields march beside a few Spanish horsemen.
shots.anim: The column grows as more warriors join from the sides.

shots.vo: Emperor Moctezuma welcomed the strangers into his city. Cortes took him hostage.
shots.visual: Moctezuma in a feathered cloak greets Cortes on the causeway; later, guards surround Moctezuma in a palace room.
shots.anim: Gifts exchanged; match cut to the same hands, now held by guards.

shots.vo: In 1520 Moctezuma was killed and the city rose up. The Spanish fled at night, so loaded with gold that some drowned in the canals. They called it the Sad Night.
shots.visual: Night on the causeway in rain; Spaniards fall into dark water clutching gold.
shots.anim: Rain, torches, splashes; a gold bar sinks slowly.

shots.vo: But they had left something behind: smallpox. The people of the Americas had never met it. It killed a huge part of the city, including the new emperor.
shots.visual: A quiet house in Tenochtitlan; a family nursing the sick by a small fire.
shots.anim: Very still; the fire dims; slow fade.

shots.vo: In 1521, after a siege of about three months, Tenochtitlan fell. On its ruins the Spanish built Mexico City.
shots.visual: The city in smoke; then the same view with a cathedral rising where the temple stood.
shots.anim: Smoke clears into a match dissolve: temple becomes cathedral.

shots.vo: Ten years later Francisco Pizarro did something similar in Peru. The Inca Empire stretched for thousands of kilometres along the Andes, and it had just been torn by a civil war between two brothers.
shots.visual: Pizarro's small band climbs a mountain road; below, Inca roads and terraces stretch into the clouds.
shots.anim: Pan along the mountain road; clouds drift below.

shots.vo: In 1532, at Cajamarca, about a hundred and seventy Spaniards ambushed the emperor Atahualpa in a town square and took him prisoner.
shots.visual: A square surrounded by low buildings; Atahualpa on a golden litter; guns and horses burst out of doorways.
shots.anim: Calm, then a gunshot; horses charge from the shadows.

shots.vo: Atahualpa offered a deal. He would fill a room with gold once, and twice with silver, if they let him go. The treasure came. They killed him anyway.
shots.visual: A stone room slowly filling with gold objects up to a line on the wall; Atahualpa watching.
shots.anim: Time-lapse: gold rises to the painted line; cut to an empty room.

shots.vo: By the 1540s Spain ruled two huge viceroyalties, New Spain from Mexico City and Peru from Lima. Most of the Americas' people had died, mainly from disease.
shots.visual: Map: two great blocks of Spanish colour in North and South America; Mexico City and Lima marked.
shots.anim: Colour spreads; a quiet population counter falls.

shots.vo: In 1545 the Spanish found the Cerro Rico at Potosi, a mountain full of silver, almost four thousand metres up in the Andes.
shots.visual: Back at the red mountain; a crowded mining town at its foot, the highest big city in the world.
shots.anim: Camera climbs from the town up the mountain slope.

shots.vo: They forced Indigenous villages to send men to work in the mines under a system called the mita. Many never came home.
shots.visual: Men climbing down narrow tunnels by candlelight, carrying heavy sacks of ore on their backs.
shots.anim: Candle flames flicker; a ladder creaks; breathing.

shots.vo: The silver was melted, stamped into coins and shipped to Spain in huge treasure fleets, guarded by warships against pirates.
shots.visual: A mint stamping coins; then a fleet of galleons in formation at sea.
shots.anim: Hammer strikes coin; match cut to a fleet sailing in line.

shots.vo: Another route went west. From 1565 the Manila galleons carried Mexican silver across the Pacific to the Philippines, to buy Chinese silk and porcelain.
shots.visual: Map: a line from Acapulco to Manila to China; silver goes one way, silk and porcelain come back.
shots.anim: Galleon icon crosses the Pacific; goods swap at Manila.

shots.vo: The Spanish silver coin, the piece of eight, was used from China to Europe. It became one of the first truly global currencies. The American dollar was based on it.
shots.visual: The corner coin grows to full frame; hands from many lands pass it along.
shots.anim: Coin passes from a Chinese merchant to a Dutch trader to an American colonist.

shots.vo: But so much silver poured into Europe that prices kept rising for a century. Spain had the money, but it did not build much with it.
shots.visual: A Spanish market where a loaf of bread costs more coins each year.
shots.anim: Coins stack higher next to the same loaf.

shots.vo: In 1516 the grandson of Ferdinand and Isabella became king. Charles the First of Spain also inherited Austria, the Netherlands and parts of Italy, and was elected Holy Roman Emperor as Charles the Fifth.
shots.visual: Young Charles, with the famous Habsburg jaw, crowned twice in two halls.
shots.anim: Two crowns lower in a split screen; his jaw juts in profile.

shots.vo: His lands circled the globe. When the sun set on Spain, it was rising on Spanish lands in the Americas or Asia.
shots.visual: A globe turns; the night shadow sweeps over it but always some Spanish colour is in sunlight.
shots.anim: Globe turns; the sunlit edge always touches Spanish colour.

shots.vo: His son Philip the Second made Madrid the capital in 1561 and built El Escorial, a palace and monastery so big it has thousands of doors and windows.
shots.visual: Philip II in black at a desk in El Escorial's huge grey courtyard.
shots.anim: Camera pulls back from his desk until he is tiny in the building.

shots.vo: He fought everyone. In 1571 his fleet, with Venice and the Pope, beat the Ottomans at Lepanto. In 1580 he took Portugal and its empire too.
shots.visual: Galleys ramming each other at Lepanto; then a Portuguese crown placed on Philip's desk.
shots.anim: Smoke and oars; cut to the crown sliding onto the desk.

shots.vo: But Protestant rebels in the Netherlands fought him for eighty years. And Protestant England kept attacking his treasure ships.
shots.visual: Dutch rebels on a dyke; an English privateer firing on a Spanish galleon.
shots.anim: Cannon flash; splinters; the corner coin wobbles.

shots.vo: In 1588 Philip sent the Armada, about one hundred and thirty ships, to invade England.
shots.visual: A crescent of galleons on a grey sea, red crosses on the sails.
shots.anim: Wide crane over the crescent formation.

shots.vo: English fire ships broke the formation, and storms did the rest. The fleet was blown around the north of Scotland and Ireland. Perhaps half the ships came home.
shots.visual: Burning ships drift toward the fleet at night; later, galleons wrecked on rocky Irish shores.
shots.anim: Fire ships glow; ships scatter; waves smash a hull on rocks.

shots.vo: Philip stopped paying his debts four times: in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596. The silver came in, and it went straight out again to pay for wars.
shots.visual: Silver bars carried in one door of the treasury and straight out the other to soldiers.
shots.anim: Conveyor of silver through the room; a stamp hits BANKRUPT four times.

shots.vo: This was also Spain's Golden Age of art. Cervantes wrote Don Quixote. Velazquez painted Las Meninas. The empire was rich in culture even as it went broke.
shots.visual: Cervantes writing by candlelight; Velazquez at his huge canvas with the little princess and her maids.
shots.anim: Quill scratches; brush strokes; the painting's light shifts.

shots.vo: In the 1600s the decline came fast. Portugal broke away in 1640. Catalonia revolted. France beat Spain's famous infantry at Rocroi in 1643.
shots.visual: Three quick scenes: Portuguese crowds cheering a new king; Catalan rebels; Spanish pikemen falling at Rocroi.
shots.anim: Three hard cuts on drum hits.

shots.vo: The royal family had married cousins for generations to keep power in the family. The last Habsburg king, Charles the Second, was sickly all his life and had no children.
shots.visual: A family tree that loops back into itself; Charles II, pale and frail, on a big throne.
shots.anim: The tree's branches knot; the throne looks too big for him.

shots.vo: When he died in 1700, Europe went to war over who would get Spain. The French Bourbon prince Philip won the crown, but Britain took Gibraltar and kept it.
shots.visual: Kings of Europe pulling at a map of Spain; a British flag planted on Gibraltar.
shots.anim: Hands tug the map; the rock gets its flag.

shots.vo: In 1808 Napoleon tricked the Spanish royal family into giving up the throne and made his brother Joseph king. On the second of May the people of Madrid rose up.
shots.visual: Madrid street fight: civilians with knives and sticks against French cavalry.
shots.anim: Chaotic street fight; the frame shakes.

shots.vo: The next day the French shot hundreds of prisoners. The painter Goya made it immortal: a man in a white shirt, arms raised, in front of the firing squad.
shots.visual: Goya's composition re-staged in the painterly style: a lantern, a man in white with raised arms, a line of soldiers.
shots.anim: Lantern light pulses; hold; cut to black on the volley.

shots.vo: With Spain itself occupied, the colonies in the Americas began to rule themselves. Simon Bolivar in the north, Jose de San Martin in the south.
shots.visual: Map: independence fires spark across South and Central America.
shots.anim: Sparks spread and colours change country by country.

shots.vo: In 1824 the last big royalist army in South America surrendered after the battle of Ayacucho in Peru. Mexico was already gone. Almost the whole mainland empire was lost.
shots.visual: A high Andean valley; royalist soldiers lay down their weapons.
shots.anim: Flags lowered; the map's Spanish colour drains from the mainland.

shots.vo: What was left were islands: Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines. Cuba was the jewel, rich from sugar, and its people wanted freedom.
shots.visual: Map zooms to three small spots of Spanish colour.
shots.anim: The map shrinks to three glowing dots.

shots.vo: In 1895 Cuba rose in revolt. The United States, ninety miles away, watched closely. American newspapers printed shocking stories every day to sell more copies.
shots.visual: Sugar fields in flames; in New York, newsboys shout headlines.
shots.anim: Fire spreads across the cane; papers fly off a press.

shots.vo: On the fifteenth of February 1898, the American warship USS Maine blew up in Havana harbour. Two hundred and sixty-six men died. Nobody proved what caused it, but the US blamed Spain.
shots.visual: Night in Havana harbour; the Maine explodes in a huge flash; the city lit up.
shots.anim: Calm water; sudden blast; shockwave ripples.

shots.vo: In May, an American squadron destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay in a single morning. In July, the Spanish fleet off Cuba tried to break out and was wiped out too.
shots.visual: Old wooden-decked Spanish ships burning against new grey American steel warships.
shots.anim: Steel ships fire in sequence; wooden ships burn.

shots.vo: In the Treaty of Paris in December 1898, Spain gave up Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. The US paid twenty million dollars for the Philippines.
shots.visual: Diplomats at a long table in Paris; a cheque for $20,000,000 slides across.
shots.anim: Cheque slides; pens sign; the last three dots on the map change colour.

shots.vo: In Spain they called it simply the Disaster. Four hundred years after Columbus, the empire that began with a lucky mistake was gone.
shots.visual: The silver coin in the corner stops spinning and falls flat with a dull clink.
shots.anim: Coin wobbles, falls, stops. Silence.

shots.vo: And without an empire, Spain turned on itself. Within forty years it would be in one of the bloodiest civil wars of the century.
shots.visual: A Madrid street in the 1930s: people on opposite sides of the street glaring at each other.
shots.anim: Slow push between the two groups as the light goes red.

hooks: 170 men captured an emperor of 10 million. Then Spain lost it all. Here's how you build and break an empire.
You use a currency that started in a Bolivian silver mine. Here's how Spain built it, then lost everything.

fixes: Potosi: transcript says it produced '80 percent of the world's supply'; that figure is not reliable. Script says 'a huge share'.
Columbus sailed with about 90 men; landfall 12 Oct 1492 (Guanahani, named San Salvador).
Tordesillas signed 7 June 1494 between Spain and Portugal (built on papal bulls of 1493); transcript wrongly makes the Pope the treaty's broker.
Tenochtitlan population estimates vary (roughly 150,000 to 250,000); script says 'perhaps two hundred thousand'.
Cortes scuttled (sank or beached) most of his ships rather than burning them.
Moctezuma died 30 June 1520 (circumstances disputed); Noche Triste 30 June/1 July 1520. Script avoids saying who killed him.
Smallpox killed Cuitlahuac, Moctezuma's successor, in late 1520.
Tenochtitlan fell 13 Aug 1521 after a siege of about 75-93 days.
Cajamarca 16 Nov 1532, about 168 Spaniards; Atahualpa executed July 1533.
Transcript calls Pizarro's 1528 trip 'the first expedition'; skipped.
Armada about 130 ships; around 67 returned (estimates vary); script says 'perhaps half'.
Spain's Habsburg inbreeding and Charles II: kept factual, no medical claims beyond 'sickly' and 'no children'.
Utrecht 1713: Gibraltar ceded to Britain (Menorca returned later).
USS Maine: 15 Feb 1898, 266 deaths; the cause is still debated (later studies suggest an internal coal-bunker fire). Script says 'nobody proved what caused it'.
Manila Bay 1 May 1898; Santiago de Cuba 3 July 1898; Treaty of Paris 10 Dec 1898, $20 million for the Philippines; Guam also ceded.
cuts: No sponsor read. Dropped the opening area figures (square miles) and the long De Soto, Rio de la Plata and California missions section to keep the story moving.
